statement: Sulfur-isotope and redox records support a prolonged, stepwise rise of environmental oxygen rather than a single instantaneous event.
Repeated late Ediacaran body- and trace-fossil assemblages document widespread macroscopic ecosystems while many organismal affinities remain contested.
The Cambrian record combines earlier lineage divergence with later ecological and skeletal expansion visible in exceptional deposits, small shelly fossils and trace fossils.
Ordovician marine diversification involved taxonomic, ecological and biogeographic restructuring across multiple clades.
Fossil and molecular evidence place early land-plant diversification before the rise of large vascular-plant ecosystems.
Digits and weight-bearing structures evolved through a mosaic transition in animals that retained substantial aquatic adaptations.
Early amniote relationships support distinct synapsid and sauropsid branches, while several Paleozoic placements remain analysis-dependent.
High-precision geochronology constrains the end-Permian biotic crisis to a geologically brief interval.
Ecological recovery after the end-Permian extinction was heterogeneous among environments and trophic levels.
Dinosaurs originated and diversified during a prolonged Triassic radiation rather than appearing as an immediately dominant fauna.
Time-calibrated phylogenetic evidence supports an early rise and subsequent Cretaceous expansion of flowering-plant diversity.
Boundary geochemistry and impact evidence support an extraterrestrial impact as the principal trigger of the K–Pg mass extinction.
A rapid negative carbon-isotope excursion and warming coincided with major marine and terrestrial biotic responses during the PETM.
Early Eocene records support rapid perissodactyl dispersal and diversification across northern continents, with basal relationships still debated.
Antarctic glaciation, global cooling and regional immigration jointly structured Eocene–Oligocene faunal turnover.
Stable-isotope evidence documents regionally asynchronous expansion of C4-dominated vegetation near the Miocene–Pliocene transition.
Late Quaternary megafaunal losses were geographically staggered and reflect interacting human and climatic pressures.
The genus Homo dispersed in multiple waves rather than one migration, with sparse fossils limiting route-level certainty.
Perissodactyla is represented as a curated flagship package with fossil ranges kept separate from divergence estimates.
Skulls and skeletons document a rapid Eocene radiation including very large browsing forms with distinctive cranial appendages.
Palaeotherium disappears close to the Eocene–Oligocene transition; the atlas no longer extends its curated range to 23 Ma.
Short limbs, a broad trunk, high-set eyes and river-deposit occurrences support a semi-aquatic interpretation without implying all amynodonts were semi-aquatic.
New Asian fossils continue to revise paraceratheriid relationships and dispersal while supporting a giant hornless rhinocerotoid identity.
The claw-bearing limbs are observed anatomy; branch-pulling behavior remains a functional interpretation.
Low-crowned teeth and limb anatomy support a primarily browsing, three-toed horse adapted to wooded environments.
Hipparionini, not the genus Hipparion sensu stricto, is the curated entity used for the wider Old and New World three-toed horse radiation.
Hippo-like body proportions alone do not establish semi-aquatic behavior; the profile labels Teleoceras as terrestrial.
Cold-adapted body proportions and cranial morphology support a steppe–tundra grazing ecology for the woolly rhinoceros.
